why: Autoplay starts the next one before you've decided to stay. With it off, stopping is the easy part.
how: Check the settings in YouTube and any streaming app you use. Find Autoplay and switch it off.

text: Leave your phone outside the bathroom all day.
proof: Your phone, left outside the bathroom door.
why: Nobody plans to spend twenty minutes on the toilet with a feed. It just happens, a few times a day, until the phone stays out.
how: Before you go in, it goes on your desk or in your bag. Mark each trip on a note or your hand.

text: Eat lunch or dinner today with no screen in front of you.
proof: Your plate, with no phone next to it.
why: Most of your screen time sneaks in around other things. A meal is twenty minutes it doesn't get.
how: Phone in your bag or another room until the plate's empty. No video on the TV or laptop either.

text: Write down how you feel right after your longest scroll.
proof: Your note, with the time.
why: You remember scrolling as relaxing. A note written the minute you stop tells you how it actually left you, and that's harder to argue with.
how: When you finally put the phone down today, write one line: how long, and how you feel. Be honest.

text: Unfollow five accounts you only watch to get mad at.
proof: A note of the five you cut.
why: Hate-watching is still watching. It's time spent annoyed at people you'll never meet, and the app counts every second of it.
how: If you roll your eyes every time they post, unfollow. If it's someone you know, mute them instead. Stop at five.

text: Let one streak end that you only keep out of habit.
proof: A note of the streak you dropped.
why: If you only open it so the number doesn't reset, it's a chore you never signed up for.
how: A game's daily login, a daily spin, a streak with someone you never talk to. Skip today's and see if you miss it.

text: Fill one notebook page with ideas instead of scrolling.
proof: The full page.
why: Most of your ideas for things to make show up when you're bored. The feed makes sure you never are.
how: On the bus or your break, before you open an app: things to make, sell, draw or fix. Keep going till the page is full.

text: Make the thing you watch other people make.
proof: The thing you made.
why: Watching someone draw, cook or edit feels like learning. Half an hour of doing it badly teaches you more than a week of watching.
how: Think of the video you'd watch next, then skip it and try what's in it for 30 minutes with what you have.

text: Watch one whole movie with your phone in another room.
proof: The end credits on the screen.
why: If a whole movie feels too long now, that's worth noticing. Two hours on one story with no phone is practice at paying attention.
how: Pick it before you sit down. Phone on the charger in another room; texts can wait two hours.

text: Give ten minutes to the thing you scroll to avoid.
proof: The work, ten minutes in.
why: A lot of scrolling is hiding from one thing you don't want to do. Once it's started, there's less to hide from.
how: Next time you open an app to put something off, close it and give that thing ten minutes on a timer.

text: Write down what kept you up last night.
proof: Your note on last night.
why: It's usually the same thing: one more video, the chat, a game. Name it and you know what to move tonight.
how: One line: when you meant to sleep, when you actually did, and what was in between.

text: Set Downtime on your phone for 30 minutes before bed.
proof: The start time, written down.
why: Stopping at 10 is easy to decide at 8 am and hard to decide at midnight. Downtime makes the call now, so you don't have to later.
how: Settings, Screen Time, Downtime. Allow calls and texts. If a parent manages your Screen Time, ask them to set it.

text: Spend your last 20 minutes before bed off screens.
proof: What you did instead.
why: A feed never ends, so you end it at 1 am. A chapter or a page of drawing has an end, and then you sleep.
how: Phone on the charger first. Then read, draw, stretch or write tomorrow's list until lights out.

text: Fall asleep tonight with nothing playing.
proof: Your earbuds in their case before bed.
why: A video in bed always has one more after it. With nothing on, the only thing left to do is fall asleep.
how: Phone on the charger, out of reach. If it's too quiet, a fan works. Give it 20 minutes before reaching for anything.

text: Sign off from the group chat at a set time tonight.
proof: The time you set, written down.
why: The chat runs till 2 because nobody wants to leave first. Be the one who does. It'll all still be there in the morning.
how: Pick the time now. When it hits, send one plain line, like "gotta sleep, talk tomorrow," and plug the phone in.

text: Write a stop time for games or shows tonight.
proof: The sticky note with your stop time.
why: There's always a next match or a next episode, so the end has to come from you. Pick it before you start, not mid-game.
how: Put it on a sticky note on the controller, laptop or TV. When it's time, finish the round and quit.

text: Swap one game or episode for time outside.
proof: Your shoes on the ground outside.
why: Under 18, you need 60 active minutes a day; adults need about 150 a week. The game will still be there when you're back.
how: A ball, a court, a walk or a run while it's still light. Go before you sit down.

text: Write down what you tell yourself before "one more".
proof: The sentence, written down.
why: "One more" always comes with a reason: you earned it, it's early, you'll stop after this. On paper, the reason sounds weaker.
how: Tonight, when you go for another video, game or snack, stop and write the exact words in your head.

text: Look up the real odds on one pack or spin.
proof: The odds, written down.
why: Every pack or spin feels like it's about to hit. The real chance, written down in front of you, is a lot harder to believe in.
how: A game with packs, spins or loot boxes. Check its help page, or search the game name plus "drop rates."

text: Delete one app that only ever takes your money.
proof: A note naming the app.
why: Some apps are built to get small payments out of you, one pack or spin at a time. Off your phone, they can't ask.
how: A game built on packs or spins, or anything you keep paying into a few dollars at a time. Delete it today.

text: Pick one evening this week with no games, shows or feeds.
proof: The plan, with the night on it.
why: An evening with nothing planned slides into games and feeds. One planned night off shows you what else you'd do with those hours.
how: Pick the night. Write what you'll do instead: practice, a walk, a friend, a book, a project. Tell someone at home.

text: Skip energy drinks, soda and coffee after lunch.
proof: Your water bottle, end of the day.
why: Try it once and see if you fall asleep easier tonight. Then you'll know, instead of guessing why you're up at 1 am.
how: Have your last one with lunch, then only water. Tomorrow, write down when you fell asleep.

text: Clear every empty can and wrapper out of your room.
proof: The full trash bag.
why: One a day doesn't look like much until it's all in one place. Then you can see what you've been running on.
how: Check the floor, the desk, your bag and under the bed. Count the cans before they go out.

text: Walk for five minutes when the afternoon slump hits.
proof: Where you walked and for how long, written.
why: The slump is when the can, the candy or the scroll usually wins. Moving first gives you a minute to decide.
how: Take the long way between classes, or step outside on your break. Go the moment you notice it.

text: Take a way home that skips the store or gas station.
proof: Your shoes on the long way home.
why: A lot of what you grab on the way home you didn't want until you walked past it. Skip the walk past and it stays on the shelf.
how: Pick the route now, in daylight. No other way? Cross to the other side and keep your money in your bag.

text: Mute one person whose page you keep checking.
proof: A note that says 'muted', no name.
why: An ex, an old friend, someone you compare yourself to. Every check costs you a mood. Muted, the feed stops bringing them to you.
how: Mute instead of block if blocking would start drama. If you catch yourself searching their name, close the app.

text: Push your first vape, can or scroll back an hour.
proof: The time of your first one, written.
why: The first one of the day feels like it can't wait. Pushing it back shows you it can, and that's where cutting down starts.
how: Pick the one you start every day with. Add an hour to when you usually have it. Gum, water or a walk helps.

text: Find out who you'd go to for help quitting.
proof: The name or number, written down.
why: The day you want to stop, you won't feel like searching. If the name's already written down, the first step is one message.
how: A school counselor, a doctor, a coach or a quit line. Nothing to quit? Find one a friend could use.

text: Ask someone who quit something how they did it.
proof: Their best tip, written down.
why: Somebody you know already got off soda, a game, a vape or their phone. What worked for them beats any list online.
how: A parent, a coach, a coworker, an older cousin. Ask what made it stick and write down the answer.

text: Go one day without trashing anyone behind their back.
proof: A tally of times you almost did.
why: When you talk about someone who isn't there, everyone listening wonders what you say about them.
how: If it starts, change the subject or stay quiet. Mark your hand each time you catch yourself.

text: Say one good thing about someone who isn't there.
proof: A note of what you said.
why: When everyone's trashing someone, one decent sentence can turn the conversation. People remember who didn't pile on.
how: Next time a name comes up, add something true and decent. Something they're good at works.

text: Mute one group chat that's mostly about other people.
proof: A note naming the chat you muted.
why: Reading drama all night eats your time and drags you into fights that aren't yours. You can still check it when you choose.
how: Open the chat's settings and mute it. If the chat is ganging up on someone, tell an adult you trust.

text: Let one argument in the chat or comments go.
proof: What you did instead of replying.
why: You won't change their mind in a reply, and you'll think about it all night if you try. Close it and get your evening back.
how: Type the reply if you have to, then delete it. Put the phone down and go do something else.

text: Decide exactly what you'll do the next time the urge hits.
proof: Your plan, written down.
why: "I'll cut back" never says when. A plan that names the moment and what you'll do instead is one you'll remember.
how: Pick the moment it hits hardest. Write one line, like "When a match ends and I want another, I stand up."

text: Put the thing you overdo somewhere hard to reach.
proof: The closed drawer or shelf it's in.
why: Habits run on whatever's closest. Put it a few rooms away and a lot of the time you won't bother going to get it.
how: Controller in the closet, snacks on the top shelf, laptop in another room. Do it now, not when you want it.

text: Go one full day without your worst habit.
proof: A note at bedtime: what was hardest.
why: One day shows you exactly where it was hiding: the bus, after dinner, in bed. You can't see that while you're still doing it.
how: Pick one, like the scroll, the can or the game. It's only until bedtime, so note the moments it gets hard.

text: Tell one person what you're cutting back on.
proof: A note of what they said.
why: Once someone knows, sliding back without anyone noticing gets harder. They might even want to cut the same thing.
how: Keep it to one line, like "I'm off energy drinks this week." Pick someone you'll see again soon.

text: Stick your reason for cutting back where you'll see it.
proof: The note, stuck in its spot.
why: When the urge hits, you forget why you wanted to stop. A note on the mirror or the console reminds you right then.
how: One line in your own words: what you want the time or money for instead. Mirror, door, console or charger.

text: Wait ten minutes before the next scroll, can or game.
proof: What you did while you waited.
why: You'll find out if you actually wanted it or just reached on reflex. Sometimes ten minutes is all it takes to stop caring.
how: Scroll, can, snack, game: when you reach, set a ten-minute timer and do something else until it rings.

text: Turn one goal into something only you control.
proof: The old goal and the new one.
why: 'Make the team' is up to a coach. 'Shoot 100 a day' is up to you. Spend today on the version you can check off tonight.
how: Pick one thing you want: a better grade, more hours, a first sale. Write the daily action for it and do it today.

text: Don't check grades, scores or views until tonight.
proof: Tonight's check time, written on paper.
why: Checking again doesn't change the number. It just hands your mood to something you can't control, over and over, all day.
how: Move those apps to your last screen. Write the one time tonight you'll look, and look only then.

text: Go the whole day without complaining out loud.
proof: Your tally of the times you slipped.
why: Complaining about the bus or the shift changes nothing about either. Each one you catch is a thing to fix or a thing to drop.
how: Mark a scrap of paper each time you slip. Telling someone about a real problem doesn't count.

text: Plan how you'll handle the person who gets to you.
proof: Your plan, initials only.
why: You already know who's going to get on your nerves today. Decide now how you'll act, so they don't get to decide it for you.
how: Write their initials and one thing you'll do instead of snapping back. If it's bullying, tell someone in charge.

text: Make someone's morning easier before you leave.
proof: What you did, like the refilled water jug.
why: Everyone you live with is rushing too. One small thing done without being asked makes the morning easier for all of you.
how: Refill the water, take out the trash, wipe the counter, make extra toast. Don't mention it.

text: Pick your biggest worry and do one thing about it.
proof: The worry and the step, written down.
why: Worrying feels like doing something, but it changes nothing. Ten minutes of action on it usually quiets it more than an hour of thinking.
how: Write the worry in one line. Under it, the smallest step you can take today. Telling someone counts. Then take it.

text: Do your part well even if the others slack.
proof: Your finished part.
why: You can't make anyone else pull their weight. Your part is the one piece you control, so make it good and get it done first.
how: A group project, side work on your shift, a chore you split. Do your piece first, then ask what's left.

text: Fix one thing from the last feedback you got.
proof: The thing you fixed.
why: Feedback stings, then most people forget it. Fixing one piece is how a comment that hurt ends up making you better at the thing.
how: Think of the last note from a teacher, coach or boss. Pick the smallest piece of it and fix only that.

text: Ask someone further along about a time they failed.
proof: Your notes on their story.
why: Almost everyone who's doing well has a story about it going badly first. Hearing one in person makes your own setbacks look normal.
how: An older teammate, a coach, a shift lead, someone in your family. Ask what went wrong and what they did next.

text: Write a thank-you note for one specific thing.
proof: The note, folded, before you hand it over.
why: A specific thank-you is rare, so people remember it. 'Thanks for staying late to help me' lands harder than 'thanks for everything.'
how: The coach, the cook, the bus driver, a parent. Two lines on what they did and what it changed. Then hand it over.

text: Clean up a mess you didn't make.
proof: The spot you cleaned.
why: Nobody will know it was you. Do it anyway, and you'll know you're not only decent when someone's watching.
how: The lunch table, the bus seat, the break room, the kitchen counter. Five minutes, then walk away.

text: Give someone credit in front of others for their part.
proof: A note of what you said.
why: Giving credit away costs you nothing, and people remember who said their name in front of everyone.
how: A teammate's pass, a classmate's idea in the group project, the coworker who covered for you. One sentence, out loud.

text: Congratulate someone who beat you or got what you wanted.
proof: Their initials and what you said.
why: Being jealous doesn't change the result. It just eats your day. Saying it out loud lets you drop it and get back to your own work.
how: The one who got your spot, your shift or the better grade, or anyone with a recent win. Keep it short and mean it.

text: Give something you don't use to someone who will.
proof: The thing, ready to give.
why: It's doing nothing at the back of your closet. In the hands of someone who'll use it, it's worth something again.
how: Clothes, a game, gear that doesn't fit. Ask whoever paid for it, then give it to a friend, a sibling or a donation bin.

text: Take the job nobody else wants today.
proof: The job, done.
why: Someone always ends up doing it, and arguing over who takes longer than the job. People notice who never dodges the boring part.
how: Picking up balls after practice, the dull part of the group project, closing duty on your shift. Say 'I've got it.'

text: Write a kind reason for one thing that annoyed you.
proof: The reason, written down.
why: You don't know why they were late, rude or short with you. Picking the generous version costs nothing and keeps the rest of your day yours.
how: The first time someone gets to you today, write what they did, then one decent reason they might have had.

text: Play or practice against someone better than you.
proof: The court, field or board afterward.
why: Beating people you already beat teaches you nothing new. Losing to someone better shows you exactly what to work on next.
how: A pickup game, one-on-one with a better teammate, chess with the friend who always wins. Ask them for one tip after.

text: Ask the person who told you no what would change it.
proof: Your notes on what they said.
why: After a cut, a bad grade or a no at home or work, the person who decided already knows what would change it. Arguing won't get you that.
how: Keep it to one calm question: 'What would you need to see from me next time?' Write the answer down after.

text: Write the worst case for something you're dreading.
proof: The worst case and your plan.
why: Dread is worse when it's vague. Written down, the worst case is usually something you'd get through, and now you have a plan for it.
how: A test, a tryout, asking for something. Write the worst that could happen, then exactly what you'd do next.

text: Write three things you'd miss if they were gone.
proof: The list of three.
why: You stop noticing what you have every day. Picturing it gone for a minute brings it back into view.
how: Be specific. Not 'friends' but the one who saved you a seat. Not 'food' but the leftovers in the fridge.

text: Write a three-step plan for your next bad day.
proof: Your three steps.
why: On a bad day you don't think clearly. Steps you wrote on a calm day do the thinking for you.
how: Think of your last bad day: what made it worse, what helped. Turn each into a step, like 'Sleep on it before I reply.'

text: Write today's worst moment as plain facts, nothing added.
proof: The plain-facts version, on paper.
why: 'My day is ruined' and 'the bus was late and I missed first period' feel different. You can do something about the second one.
how: Two sentences: what happened and what it cost you. Leave out 'always', 'never' and 'ruined'.

text: Write down a hard thing you've already gotten through.
proof: The page, face down.
why: You've already handled things you once thought you couldn't. How you did it is something you can use on what's in front of you now.
how: Pick one you're okay thinking about. Write what happened, then what you did. Circle what you could use this week.

text: Say the apology you've been putting off.
proof: Your note of what you said.
why: An apology gets harder the longer you wait, and they usually know you owe it. Saying it straight clears it for both of you.
how: Write it first: what you did, sorry, what you'll do now. No 'but'. Then say it in person or on a call.

text: List what you can do now that you couldn't last year.
proof: Your list.
why: Next to people online you always look behind. Next to last year, you can see exactly what you've built.
how: Skills, school or work, sports, money, people. If you get stuck before three, ask someone who knows you.

text: Write what you'd tell a friend with your problem.
proof: The advice, written down.
why: From the inside, your own problem feels tangled. Written as advice for someone else, the next step is usually easier to see.
how: Start with 'Here's what I'd do.' Write five lines, then read them back like they're for you.

text: Wait an hour before you answer a text that annoys you.
proof: Your reply, drafted on paper first.
why: Replies sent while you're mad are the ones that get screenshotted. An hour later you can still say it, just in a way you won't regret.
how: Write your reply on paper first. Set a one-hour timer. Read it again before you send anything.

text: Redo the questions you missed on your last test.
proof: The missed questions, redone.
why: The grade is done and you can't change it. Fixing what you missed is the part that changes the next one.
how: Dig out the last test, or a task you got corrected on at work. Redo each miss until you could explain it.

text: Sit for ten minutes with no phone, music or screen.
proof: The spot where you sat.
why: Most hard work feels boring at first, and your phone is always there to rescue you. Ten minutes of nothing makes boredom easier to sit through.
how: Set a ten-minute timer and leave the phone in another room. Sit somewhere and let your mind wander till it rings.

text: Spend an hour on something someone said you couldn't do.
proof: What you did in that hour.
why: Arguing with them won't change their mind. An hour of work changes what you can actually do, and that part is yours.
how: The jump shot, the drawings, the class, the business idea. Phone in another room, an hour on the timer. Start.

text: Keep one promise today that you'd rather get out of.
proof: A note of the promise, checked off.
why: Anyone keeps their word when it's easy. Keeping it when you'd rather bail is how people learn they can count on you.
how: The shift you said you'd cover, the help you offered, the plan you agreed to. Show up on time, as promised.

text: Make a plan to try again at something you didn't get.
proof: The plan, with a date on it.
why: A no is one person's answer on one day. A plan with a date turns it into your next try instead of the end of it.
how: A team, a job, a part, a school, a sale. Write what you'd change, and the day you'll try again.

text: Walk away for ten minutes the next time you get heated.
proof: Your note on what set you off.
why: What you say in the first minute of being mad is usually what you end up apologizing for. Ten minutes away and you'll handle it better.
how: A game, an argument at home, a bad call at practice. Say 'give me a minute', walk off, come back when you're calm.

text: Write down one thing you want only because others have it.
proof: The page.
why: There's always a next thing everyone has. Writing what you'd actually do with it shows how much of the want is just keeping up.
how: Shoes, a phone, an outfit, a trip. Write it down, then what you'd really do with it. Be honest.

text: Write down five people who've helped you, and how.
proof: The list, initials only.
why: Seeing the names tells you who to thank, and who to call the next time it gets hard.
how: Teachers, coaches, a parent, the coworker who showed you how. One line each on what they did.

text: Write down the criticism that stung and what's useful in it.
proof: The page, folded in half.
why: Most criticism is part useful and part noise. Pull out the useful part and the rest loses most of its sting.
how: Write what they said. Underline only the part you could use. If it was just an insult, there's nothing to keep.

text: Before bed, write what you'll do differently tomorrow.
proof: Tonight's three lines.
why: If you never look back at a day, you'll keep repeating it. Five minutes at night shows you exactly what to fix tomorrow.
how: Three lines: what went well, what didn't, what you'll change tomorrow. No full sentences needed.

text: Write the last argument from the other person's side.
proof: Their side, in your handwriting.
why: You already know your side by heart. Writing theirs shows you what you missed, and it usually makes the fix obvious.
how: Five sentences, written as them, starting with 'I was upset because'. Be fair, even if they weren't.

text: Check in on a friend who's been quiet lately.
proof: Their initials and when you talked.
why: People having a hard time often go quiet instead of asking. A plain 'you good' from you might be the only one they get.
how: Call or talk in person. Mostly listen. If they mention hurting themselves, get help right away: call or text 988.

text: Write down a grudge, then tear it up.
proof: The torn-up page.
why: Staying mad usually costs you more than it costs them. Writing it all out gets it out of your head, so you can decide what to do about it.
how: Write everything you'd say to them. Read it once, then tear it up. If you still need to talk, do it calm, tomorrow.

text: Write what you were stressed about a year ago.
proof: The list, with how each turned out.
why: Most of it probably doesn't matter anymore. Today's problem will likely go the same way, so give it the attention it's worth and no more.
how: Think back to this time last year: school, a fight, money, a game. Next to each, write how it turned out.

text: Spend 45 minutes on the thing you're scared will flop.
proof: What you made in 45 minutes.
why: How people react isn't in your control. Whether the thing exists is, and nothing gets better before it exists.
how: The design, the page of drawings, the business idea. Phone in another room, timer on, make a rough first version.

text: Stop waiting for gear and start with what you have.
proof: What you made with what you had.
why: Waiting for the right camera, tablet or shoes is an easy way to never start. What you make with what you have shows you what you actually need.
how: Phone camera, pencil and paper, a ball, the floor of your room. Give it 30 minutes tonight and finish something.

text: Write a note to yourself to open next year.
proof: The folded note, with next year's date.
why: A year from now, today's problems will look different. Writing them down now lets you check how they turned out and how far you got.
how: What's on your mind, what you're working on, one thing you want done by then. Fold it, date it, put it away.

text: Ask someone you live with about their day, and listen.
proof: One thing they told you, written down.
why: The people you live with mostly get your tired, end-of-day self. Ten minutes of real listening gives them a better one.
how: After dinner or when they get home. Phone face down. Ask one follow-up question before you talk about you.
